beats.intro: Chapter six. [[sub]]An index is a yardstick for a market. This chapter shows how indexes are built, and why the construction choices change the answer.
beats.returns: A security market index measures a target market. Its constituents are chosen to represent that market. [[start]]Say an index starts at one thousand. [[price]]If the constituents rise five percent, a price return index shows one thousand fifty. It counts only price changes. [[total]]But the constituents also paid dividends of two percent. A total return index reinvests that income, and stands near one thousand seventy. [[note]]Same securities, same weights, different numbers. Price return shows price movement. Total return measures what investors actually earned.
beats.weighting: Weighting is the key construction choice. Take three stocks. [[table]]A rises twenty percent, from ten to twelve. B falls ten percent, from thirty to twenty seven. C rises ten percent, from sixty to sixty six. [[pw]]Price weighting adds the prices and divides. The index goes from thirty three point three three to thirty five. Up five percent. High-priced stocks matter more. [[ew]]Equal weighting gives each stock the same weight, so the index return is the average return: six point seven percent. [[mc]]Market-cap weighting weights by total value, price times shares. The total goes from thirty seven hundred to thirty eight seventy: up four point six percent. Larger companies matter more. [[note]]Same stocks, three different answers.
beats.altweights: Two refinements. [[float]]Float-adjusted weighting counts only the shares available to the investing public. If sixty percent of a thousand dollar company floats, it counts as six hundred. Most market-cap indexes are float adjusted. [[drawback]]But market-cap weighting has a drawback. Stocks that have risen get bigger weights, and stocks that have fallen get smaller ones. It behaves a little like a momentum strategy. [[fund]]Fundamental weighting uses size measures that do not depend on price, such as earnings, dividends, or book value. Two companies earn twenty each, but A is worth two hundred, and B eight hundred. Market-cap weights are twenty and eighty percent. Earnings weights are fifty and fifty, so the cheaper stock, A, gets more weight.
beats.management: Indexes need maintenance. [[reb]]Rebalancing restores target weights. In an equal-weighted index, stocks that rose become too large, and are trimmed back. [[recon]]Reconstitution changes the constituents, so the index keeps representing its target market. Some companies leave, and new ones join. [[turn]]Both create turnover. And reconstitution can move prices, since funds that track the index must buy the additions, and sell the deletions.
beats.uses: Indexes serve many purposes. [[sent]]They gauge market sentiment. [[bench]]They are benchmarks for actively managed portfolios. [[risk]]They proxy for systematic risk, so risk-adjusted performance can be measured. [[alloc]]They stand in for asset classes in asset allocation models. [[prod]]And they are the blueprint for index funds and exchange traded funds.
beats.types: Indexes exist for every asset class, each with its own challenges. [[eq]]Equity indexes cut the market by region, size, sector and style. Style indexes churn more. [[fi]]Fixed income: thousands of securities, which mature and are replaced, trade in dealer markets, and are often illiquid. [[com]]Commodity indexes hold futures contracts, so returns include the roll yield, and differ from spot prices. [[re]]Real estate indexes can be appraisal based, repeat sales, or REIT indexes. Only REIT indexes are priced continuously. [[hf]]Hedge funds choose which database to report to, so there is survivorship bias. The constituents determine the index.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]A price return index counts price changes. A total return index adds reinvested income. [[w2]]Weighting changes the result: price, equal, market-cap, float-adjusted or fundamental. [[w3]]Rebalancing restores weights. Reconstitution changes constituents. Both create turnover. [[w4]]Before using an index, understand how it is constructed.
